analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agencies to repeal two existing rules before issuing any new costly rule.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have required agencies to repeal two rules for every new costly rule they issued, never received a hearing or vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The One In, Two Out Act would bar any federal agency from issuing a new rule that costs businesses or governments money unless the agency first repeals two existing rules. For expensive 'major' rules (those with roughly $100 million or more in annual impact), the White House budget office would have to certify that the new rule costs no more than the ones being repealed. The effect is a hard cap on federal regulation: agencies could only add rules by cutting them.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that are subject to federal regulation — manufacturers, energy companies, financial firms, and others — would gain, because the total cost and number of federal rules could only shrink. Some of those savings could reach consumers through lower prices, but the main gain goes to regulated industries in the form of lower compliance costs and fewer new obligations.

how_it_helps.text: No agency could issue a new rule that imposes a cost or responsibility on businesses, individuals, or state and local governments without first repealing two existing rules, shrinking the total body of regulation.

For major rules — generally those with $100 million or more in annual economic impact — the agency would also have to show the new rule's cost is no greater than the cost of the rules it repealed, with the White House regulatory office certifying that math.
Rules being relaxed to become less burdensome are exempt from the offset requirement, so the bill removes rules in one direction only.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost in the form of rules that are never written: new health, safety, consumer, and competition protections generally impose costs on companies, and under this bill they could only be issued if paired with repeals elsewhere. The bill's count-based formula requires agencies to trade rules against rules rather than weigh a rule's benefits against its costs, so protections against emerging hazards could be blocked until agencies find two unrelated rules to sacrifice.

drawbacks.text: The formula counts rules, not consequences: it requires repealing two rules regardless of whether the new rule prevents far greater harm — a major new safety or competition rule could be blocked unless two unrelated rules are scrapped, even if the new rule's benefits dwarf its costs.

The offset mechanism could force agencies to repeal still-needed protections to act on new problems, and the exemptions (internal agency policy and procurement) mean agencies could still grow in ways that don't count against the cap.

A supporter would argue federal rules impose real compliance costs that are passed to consumers, and that a cap forces agencies to prioritize; the counterweight is that a two-for-one requirement applies a rigid accounting rule in place of case-by-case judgment about whether a rule is worthwhile.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Businesses would see lower compliance costs, and some of that could reach consumers. But the bill's own design — trading rule counts instead of weighing benefits against costs, and requiring cost-neutrality only on the cost side of the ledger — makes it structurally difficult for agencies to issue any significant new protection, whatever its merit. The savings are real but uneven; the foregone protections would fall on workers, consumers, and small governments least equipped to judge them.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee from the day it was introduced — first in Oversight and Reform and Judiciary, then in a Judiciary subcommittee — and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael McCaul introduced the One In, Two Out Act on May 13, 2021, joined by Rep. Chip Roy; one Republican cosponsor is listed on the bill.
The bill was referred the same day to the Committee on Oversight and Reform and the Committee on the Judiciary.
On November 9, 2021, the Judiciary portion was referred to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law, and no further action was recorded.
The bill never advanced out of committee or to a floor vote in either chamber before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, federal agencies kept their existing authority to weigh rules on their merits, and the regulatory protections in place at the time remained. The bill's would-have-been beneficiaries — regulated industries facing a mandatory shrinkage of federal rules — gained nothing, and neither did anyone else; the main significance is that a structural cap on regulation was never adopted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; no one materially gained

for.name: Rep. Chip Roy
for.what_they_did: Joined McCaul in introducing the bill and is its sole listed cosponsor.

against.name: House Oversight and Reform Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing or markup after its May 2021 referral.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Sent the bill to a subcommittee in November 2021 and took no further recorded action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by two House Republicans with only a Republican cosponsor listed and no recorded Democratic support; no votes occurred, so the record shows a one-party effort that did not advance.

industries.industry: Regulated industries generally (manufacturing, energy, finance, and other rule-bound businesses)
industries.note: The bill died in committee, so businesses gained nothing, but the bill as written would have reduced their compliance obligations by capping the total number and cost of federal rules. Its benefit to these industries would come largely at the cost of future public protections.

industries.industry: Agencies issuing competition and antitrust rules
industries.note: The bill was referred to the Judiciary subcommittee handling antitrust law, indicating it would constrain agencies like the FTC: any new competition rule imposing costs would have required two repeals first.

Agencies would have operated under a two-for-one rule and a White House cost certification for major rules, sharply limiting their discretion, while remaining exempt for internal policy and procurement rules.
